title: City vs Countryside
subtitle: Weigh up urban life, rural life and remote work with balanced, real arguments

lessons.title: Vivre en ville
lessons.description: Talk about the advantages and drawbacks of city life, its cost and its daily rhythm.

blocks.heading: Ce que la ville offre
blocks.body: City life is usually defended with the same three arguments: things are close by, there is always something to do, and opportunities — jobs, studies, culture — are concentrated in one place. «À portée de main» (within reach) and «tout est à côté» capture that sense of convenience well.

examples.french: Léna a choisi Lyon pour les opportunités professionnelles.
examples.english: Léna chose Lyon for the job opportunities.

examples.french: Ici, tout est à portée de main : le travail, les commerces, les amis.
examples.english: Here, everything is within reach: work, shops, friends.

examples.french: Il y a toujours quelque chose à faire, même un mardi soir.
examples.english: There is always something to do, even on a Tuesday evening.

examples.french: Les transports en commun sont pratiques, on n'a pas besoin de voiture.
examples.english: Public transport is convenient, you don't need a car.

examples.french: La diversité des quartiers, c'est ce qui me plaît le plus.
examples.english: The diversity of the neighbourhoods is what I like most.

blocks.tip: «À côté» just means «nearby», not literally «next to»: «Le cinéma est à côté» = the cinema is close by.

blocks.heading: Ce que la ville coûte
blocks.body: The other side of the argument is cost and pressure. Loyer, stress and bruit come back constantly in French conversations about cities. Notice how speakers soften complaints with «un peu» or «quand même» rather than stating them flatly — it keeps the tone balanced rather than bitter.

examples.french: Le loyer prend presque la moitié de mon salaire.
examples.english: The rent takes up almost half my salary.

examples.french: C'est un peu bruyant, surtout le week-end.
examples.english: It's a bit noisy, especially on weekends.

examples.french: On respire quand même moins bien qu'ailleurs, à cause de la pollution.
examples.english: You still breathe a bit worse than elsewhere, because of the pollution.

examples.french: Le stress fait partie du quotidien, je crois qu'on s'y habitue.
examples.english: Stress is part of daily life — I think you get used to it.

examples.french: Un appartement correct reste difficile à trouver et cher.
examples.english: A decent apartment is still hard to find and expensive.

blocks.tip: «Quand même» softens a complaint into an observation: «C'est cher, quand même» sounds less like a grievance than «C'est trop cher.»

blocks.heading: Le rythme d'une journée en ville
blocks.body: Urban routines are shaped by transport and schedules: the metro at a fixed time, a commute measured in minutes, lunch squeezed into an hour. French uses «serré» (tight) a lot for this kind of pace, and «à l'heure de pointe» for rush hour.

examples.french: Le matin, tout est serré : le métro, le café, la réunion de neuf heures.
examples.english: In the morning, everything is tight: the metro, the coffee, the nine o'clock meeting.

examples.french: À l'heure de pointe, le trajet double de durée.
examples.english: At rush hour, the commute takes twice as long.

examples.french: Elle prend le même bus tous les jours, à la minute près.
examples.english: She takes the same bus every day, down to the minute.

examples.french: Le soir, on rentre tard et on a peu de temps libre.
examples.english: In the evening, you get home late and have little free time.

examples.french: Le week-end, on essaie de profiter du quartier pour ralentir un peu.
examples.english: On weekends, you try to enjoy the neighbourhood to slow down a bit.

blocks.tip: «À la minute près» is a handy exaggeration for describing a very tight, precise routine.

blocks.heading: Les pronoms relatifs : qui, que, où, dont
blocks.body: Describing a city well means linking short facts into one fluid sentence instead of stacking short ones. Use qui when the relative is the subject, que when it is the object, où for a place, and dont when the following verb or noun needs de (parler de, avoir besoin de, se plaindre de, le prix de…).

examples.french: C'est un quartier qui a beaucoup changé en dix ans.
examples.english: It's a neighbourhood that has changed a lot in ten years.

examples.french: Le loyer que je paie a doublé depuis mon arrivée.
examples.english: The rent I pay has doubled since I arrived.

examples.french: C'est la rue où se trouve le marché du dimanche.
examples.english: It's the street where the Sunday market is held.

examples.french: Le bruit dont elle se plaint vient surtout du bar d'en bas.
examples.english: The noise she complains about mostly comes from the bar downstairs.

examples.french: C'est un abonnement dont je me sers tous les jours.
examples.english: It's a pass I use every day.

blocks.tip: Quick test: turn the relative clause into a full sentence. «Je me sers DE cet abonnement» → de is there, so dont; «Je paie CE loyer» → no de, so que.

blocks.heading: Nuancer : d'un côté… de l'autre, certes… mais
blocks.body: A balanced opinion in French rarely says only one thing. «D'un côté… de l'autre (côté)…» presents two facts side by side without picking a winner. «Certes… mais…» concedes a point before turning it around — useful for staying fair when comparing city and countryside.

examples.french: D'un côté, tout est pratique ; de l'autre, tout coûte cher.
examples.english: On one hand, everything is convenient; on the other, everything is expensive.

examples.french: Certes, le loyer est élevé, mais le salaire l'est aussi.
examples.english: Granted, the rent is high, but so is the salary.

examples.french: D'un côté, il y a du bruit ; de l'autre, il y a de la vie.
examples.english: On one hand there's noise; on the other, there's life.

examples.french: Certes, les embouteillages sont fatigants, mais les transports en commun compensent.
examples.english: Granted, the traffic jams are tiring, but public transport makes up for it.

examples.french: D'un côté, on est stressé ; de l'autre, on ne s'ennuie jamais.
examples.english: On one hand you're stressed; on the other, you're never bored.

blocks.tip: «Certes» always signals that a «mais» is coming — using it alone, without a follow-up, sounds unfinished to a French ear.

passages.title: La journée de Léna
passages.french:
Léna vit à Lyon depuis six ans, dans un quartier qu'elle a mis longtemps à trouver.
Son réveil sonne à sept heures, et à sept heures et demie elle est déjà dans le métro.
À l'heure de pointe, le trajet dont elle se plaint le plus dure presque quarante minutes.
Certes, c'est fatigant, mais elle aime le fait que tout soit accessible sans voiture.
La journée passe vite : réunions, déjeuner rapide, quelques messages entre deux rendez-vous.
Le soir, elle profite du quartier qu'elle a choisi pour son ambiance animée.
D'un côté, le loyer prend presque la moitié de son salaire ; de l'autre, elle ne s'ennuie jamais.
Elle aime sortir sans avoir à réserver des semaines à l'avance.
Ce qu'elle aime le moins, c'est le bruit qui monte parfois jusqu'à minuit.
Malgré cela, quand ses amis lui parlent de déménager à la campagne, elle hésite.
Elle a besoin de cette agitation, même si elle en rit un peu elle-même.
Pour elle, la ville reste un compromis, pas une évidence.
passages.english:
Léna has lived in Lyon for six years, in a neighbourhood she took a long time to find.
Her alarm goes off at seven, and by seven thirty she's already on the metro.
At rush hour, the commute she complains about most takes nearly forty minutes.
Granted, it's tiring, but she likes the fact that everything is accessible without a car.
The day goes by quickly: meetings, a quick lunch, a few messages between appointments.
In the evening, she enjoys the neighbourhood she chose for its lively atmosphere.
On one hand, the rent takes up almost half her salary; on the other, she is never bored.
She likes going out without having to book weeks in advance.
What she likes least is the noise that sometimes carries on until midnight.
Despite that, when her friends talk to her about moving to the countryside, she hesitates.
She needs that buzz, even if she laughs at herself a little for it.
For her, the city remains a compromise, not an obvious choice.

lessons.title: La campagne
lessons.description: Talk about the quality of life, distance and services that shape everyday life in the countryside.

blocks.heading: Ce que la campagne offre
blocks.body: Countryside conversations circle back to the same idea: space and calm. «Respirer», «le grand calme» and «la qualité de vie» describe something felt rather than measured. Note that «calme» works both as an adjective and, with «le», as a noun.

examples.french: Thomas s'est installé dans un village d'Ardèche il y a trois ans.
examples.english: Thomas moved to a village in the Ardèche three years ago.

examples.french: Ici, on respire, il n'y a presque pas de bruit.
examples.english: Here, you can breathe — there's almost no noise.

examples.french: Le calme du soir, c'est ce qui lui manquait le plus en ville.
examples.english: The calm of the evening is what he missed most in the city.

examples.french: La qualité de vie est meilleure, même si le salaire est plus modeste.
examples.english: The quality of life is better, even though the salary is more modest.

examples.french: Les voisins se connaissent tous et s'entraident naturellement.
examples.english: The neighbours all know each other and naturally help one another.

blocks.tip: «On respire» is used figuratively even without pollution in mind: it simply means «life feels less pressured here.»

blocks.heading: Ce que la campagne demande
blocks.body: The trade-off is distance: fewer services, and a car often becomes necessary rather than optional. French speakers use «il faut» a lot here — a light, common way to state a practical requirement without sounding dramatic.

examples.french: Il faut vingt minutes de voiture pour aller à la pharmacie.
examples.english: It takes twenty minutes by car to get to the pharmacy.

examples.french: Sans voiture, on est vite isolé.
examples.english: Without a car, you quickly become isolated.

examples.french: L'école la plus proche est à huit kilomètres.
examples.english: The nearest school is eight kilometres away.

examples.french: Le médecin ne vient qu'un jour sur deux dans le village.
examples.english: The doctor only comes every other day in the village.

examples.french: Certains soirs, la solitude se fait sentir.
examples.english: Some evenings, the loneliness is noticeable.

blocks.tip: «Il faut» + infinitive states a requirement neutrally: «il faut une heure pour…» — no subject needed, unlike «je dois».

blocks.heading: Le rythme d'une journée à la campagne
blocks.body: Rural routines follow the land and the seasons more than the clock. Farmers like Marc's neighbours talk about «se lever tôt», «les saisons» and «le potager» — daily life organised around weather and growth rather than a metro timetable.

examples.french: Ici, on se lève tôt, souvent avant le soleil.
examples.english: Here, you get up early, often before the sun.

examples.french: Le rythme change avec les saisons : plus calme l'hiver, plus chargé l'été.
examples.english: The pace changes with the seasons: quieter in winter, busier in summer.

examples.french: Thomas s'occupe de son potager tous les week-ends.
examples.english: Thomas tends his vegetable garden every weekend.

examples.french: On planifie sa semaine autour de la météo.
examples.english: You plan your week around the weather.

examples.french: Le soir, il ne se passe presque rien, et c'est reposant.
examples.english: In the evening, almost nothing happens, and it's restful.

blocks.tip: «Chargé» (busy, loaded) applies to a day, a week or a schedule, not just to objects: «une journée chargée» = a busy day.

blocks.heading: Il faut que + subjonctif
blocks.body: «Il faut que» introduces a necessity and is always followed by the subjunctive. It is one of the most common ways to state that something is required — for daily errands, for planning, for adapting to rural constraints. Regular -er verbs take the same endings as the present indicative in the nous/vous forms, but je/tu/il/elle/ils/elles borrow from the ils-form of the present.

examples.french: Il faut qu'on parte tôt pour arriver à l'heure chez le médecin.
examples.english: We have to leave early to get to the doctor's on time.

examples.french: Il faut que tu prennes la voiture, il n'y a pas de bus.
examples.english: You have to take the car, there's no bus.

examples.french: Il faut qu'on fasse les courses avant que l'épicerie ne ferme.
examples.english: We have to do the shopping before the grocery store closes.

examples.french: Il faut que je sache conduire pour vivre ici.
examples.english: I need to know how to drive to live here.

examples.french: Il faut qu'on s'organise, sinon on perd trop de temps sur la route.
examples.english: We need to get organised, or we waste too much time on the road.

blocks.tip: «Il faut» alone + infinitive (il faut partir) is used when no specific subject is named; «il faut que» + subjunctive is used once a subject appears (il faut que tu partes).

blocks.heading: Le pronom y
blocks.body: «Y» replaces a place already mentioned, or an idea introduced with à. It sits right before the verb and saves you from repeating «à la campagne», «au village», «à cette question». It is essential for talking naturally about distance and habits without sounding repetitive.

examples.french: Il vit à la campagne depuis dix ans ; il s'y sent bien.
examples.english: He's lived in the countryside for ten years; he feels good there.

examples.french: Tu vas souvent au village ? — Oui, j'y vais tous les samedis.
examples.english: Do you go to the village often? — Yes, I go there every Saturday.

examples.french: On pensait déménager, et on y pense encore.
examples.english: We were thinking of moving, and we're still thinking about it.

examples.french: La pharmacie est loin, mais on s'y habitue.
examples.english: The pharmacy is far, but you get used to it.

examples.french: Il n'y a pas grand-chose ici, mais on y trouve l'essentiel.
examples.english: There isn't much here, but you find the essentials.

blocks.tip: Don't confuse «y» (there / about it) with «il y a» (there is) — same word, different job.

passages.title: Le choix de Thomas
passages.french:
Thomas a quitté Lyon pour un village d'Ardèche il y a trois ans, sans vraiment savoir à quoi s'attendre.
La maison qu'il a trouvée donne sur un champ, et la forêt commence juste derrière.
Le matin, il se lève tôt, s'occupe un peu du potager, puis part travailler.
Il faut qu'il prenne la voiture pour tout : le travail, les courses, le médecin.
L'épicerie du village a fermé l'année dernière, alors le supermarché le plus proche est à vingt minutes.
Certes, c'est contraignant, mais il dit qu'il n'a jamais aussi bien dormi.
Ses voisins, des agriculteurs pour la plupart, l'ont accueilli sans façon.
L'entraide entre eux est réelle : on se prête des outils, on s'échange des légumes.
Le silence du soir l'a surpris au début ; maintenant, il ne s'en passerait plus.
Certains week-ends d'hiver, la solitude se fait sentir, il ne le cache pas.
Mais quand ses amis de Lyon lui parlent d'embouteillages et de loyers, il ne regrette rien.
Pour lui, la campagne a changé sa façon de vivre plus qu'il ne l'imaginait.
passages.english:
Thomas left Lyon for a village in the Ardèche three years ago, without really knowing what to expect.
The house he found looks out onto a field, and the forest starts right behind it.
In the morning, he gets up early, spends a little time in the vegetable garden, then goes to work.
He has to take the car for everything: work, shopping, the doctor.
The village grocery store closed last year, so the nearest supermarket is twenty minutes away.
Granted, it's inconvenient, but he says he has never slept so well.
His neighbours, mostly farmers, welcomed him without fuss.
The mutual help between them is real: they lend each other tools, exchange vegetables.
The silence in the evening surprised him at first; now he couldn't do without it.
Some winter weekends, the loneliness sets in — he doesn't hide it.
But when his friends from Lyon talk about traffic jams and rents, he has no regrets.
For him, the countryside changed his way of living more than he had imagined.

lessons.title: Le télétravail
lessons.description: Explore how remote work changes where you can live, and practise hypotheses with si + imparfait → conditionnel.

blocks.heading: Le télétravail change la question
blocks.body: Remote work turns «city or countryside» into a question about internet speed and flexibility rather than commute distance. Inès, who works for a company in Paris, can now consider both without changing employer.

examples.french: Depuis le télétravail, Inès n'a plus besoin d'habiter près du bureau.
examples.english: Since remote work started, Inès no longer needs to live near the office.

examples.french: Son entreprise autorise deux jours de télétravail par semaine.
examples.english: Her company allows two days of remote work per week.

examples.french: Elle peut travailler depuis n'importe où, du moment que la connexion suit.
examples.english: She can work from anywhere, as long as the connection keeps up.

examples.french: Ses collègues sont dispersés dans toute la France.
examples.english: Her colleagues are scattered all over France.

examples.french: La flexibilité, c'est ce qui a le plus changé sa vie.
examples.english: Flexibility is what has changed her life the most.

blocks.tip: «Du moment que» (as long as) introduces a simple condition, more casual than «à condition que», which needs the subjunctive.

blocks.heading: Ce qu'il faut pour bien télétravailler
blocks.body: Living far from an office sounds simple until you check the practical details: fibre internet, a quiet room, and a coworking space nearby for the days video calls pile up. These constraints matter as much as the landscape.

examples.french: Sans la fibre, le télétravail serait difficile ici.
examples.english: Without fibre internet, remote work would be difficult here.

examples.french: Le débit doit être suffisant pour les visioconférences.
examples.english: The speed has to be enough for video calls.

examples.french: Un espace de coworking a ouvert dans le village voisin.
examples.english: A coworking space has opened in the neighbouring village.

examples.french: Elle a besoin d'un bureau calme, loin du bruit de la maison.
examples.english: She needs a quiet office, away from the noise of the house.

examples.french: Le wifi coupe parfois pendant les réunions, ce qui reste frustrant.
examples.english: The wifi sometimes cuts out during meetings, which is still frustrating.

blocks.tip: «Suffisant» (sufficient) is a very B1 word for setting a practical minimum: «un débit suffisant», «un salaire suffisant».

blocks.heading: Peser une décision qui n'est pas encore prise
blocks.body: When a choice is only hypothetical, French switches naturally into si + imparfait → conditionnel: «si je déménageais, je gagnerais du temps». This lets Inès imagine outcomes without committing to them — the grammar point for this lesson.

examples.french: Si elle déménageait à la campagne, elle gagnerait du temps le matin.
examples.english: If she moved to the countryside, she'd save time in the morning.

examples.french: Si le loyer était plus bas, elle pourrait économiser davantage.
examples.english: If the rent were lower, she could save more.

examples.french: Elle hésite encore, mais elle imagine déjà les deux options.
examples.english: She's still hesitating, but she already imagines both options.

examples.french: Si elle restait en ville, elle garderait ses amis à proximité.
examples.english: If she stayed in the city, she'd keep her friends nearby.

examples.french: Rien n'est décidé : elle compare, elle pèse le pour et le contre.
examples.english: Nothing is decided: she compares, she weighs the pros and cons.

blocks.tip: «Peser le pour et le contre» (to weigh the pros and cons) is the perfect expression for a chapter about undecided hypotheses.

blocks.heading: Si + imparfait → conditionnel présent
blocks.body: To imagine a hypothetical situation and its likely result, French pairs si + imparfait in the condition with the conditionnel présent in the result. The imparfait is formed from the nous-form of the present (nous déménageons → déménag-) plus -ais, -ais, -ait, -ions, -iez, -aient. The conditionnel takes the future stem plus those same endings.

examples.french: Si elle déménageait, elle gagnerait du temps chaque matin.
examples.english: If she moved, she would save time every morning.

examples.french: Si le loyer était plus bas, elle économiserait davantage.
examples.english: If the rent were lower, she would save more.

examples.french: Si tu avais une bonne connexion, tu pourrais travailler d'ici.
examples.english: If you had a good connection, you could work from here.

examples.french: Si nous changions de vie, nous serions plus détendus.
examples.english: If we changed our lifestyle, we would be more relaxed.

examples.french: S'ils s'installaient à la campagne, ils verraient moins leurs amis.
examples.english: If they settled in the countryside, they would see their friends less.

blocks.tip: Never use «si» with a conditionnel right after it: «si j'aurais» is always wrong — it must be «si j'avais».

blocks.heading: Verbes irréguliers et nuances de l'hypothèse
blocks.body: Several very common verbs have irregular conditionnel stems worth learning by heart: être → ser-, avoir → aur-, aller → ir-, faire → fer-, pouvoir → pourr-, devoir → devr-, vouloir → voudr-. Adding «peut-être que» or «sans doute» before the result softens the prediction, which fits a decision that is still open.

examples.english: If she left, she would probably be more at ease.

examples.english: If she stayed in the city, she wouldn't have to reorganise everything.

passages.title: La décision d'Inès
passages.french:
Depuis un an, Inès télétravaille trois jours par semaine pour une entreprise parisienne.
Son appartement est petit et cher, mais elle n'a jamais vraiment envisagé de partir.
Ce qui a changé, c'est une visioconférence avec une collègue installée dans un village du Périgord.
Si le débit était suffisant là-bas, Inès pourrait sans doute faire la même chose.
Elle a commencé à peser le pour et le contre, un carnet ouvert sur la table.
Si elle déménageait, elle gagnerait du temps, de l'espace, et sans doute un peu de calme.
Mais si elle partait trop loin, elle verrait ses amis beaucoup moins souvent.
Elle a appelé son propriétaire pour vérifier si la fibre existait dans la région visée.
Elle a aussi demandé à son patron ce qu'il penserait d'un télétravail à temps plein.
Rien n'est encore décidé, mais elle imagine déjà les deux vies, presque comme un film.
Ce qu'elle sait, c'est que la ville ne serait pas un échec, ni la campagne une solution parfaite.
Pour elle, ce serait simplement un autre équilibre, ni meilleur ni pire.
passages.english:
For a year, Inès has been working remotely three days a week for a company in Paris.
Her apartment is small and expensive, but she never really considered leaving.
What changed was a video call with a colleague who had settled in a village in the Périgord.
If the connection speed were good enough there, Inès could probably do the same.
She started weighing the pros and cons, a notebook open on the table.
If she moved, she would save time, gain space, and probably a bit of calm.
But if she moved too far, she would see her friends much less often.
She called her landlord to check whether fibre internet existed in the area she had in mind.
She also asked her boss what he would think of full-time remote work.
Nothing is decided yet, but she already imagines both lives, almost like a film.
What she knows is that the city wouldn't be a failure, nor the countryside a perfect solution.
For her, it would simply be a different balance, neither better nor worse.
